title: Ta'anit and Yoma: Rain, Honi, Repentance and Yom Kippur
bigQuestion: When a rule and a human need meet head-on, how does the Talmud decide which comes first?

story.title: The Circle in the Dust
story.kicker: A dry land, a man in a circle and a prayer that some rabbis admired and others worried about.
paragraphs: The Mishnah tells of a year with no rain. In the land of Israel, rain decides everything. Without it, the wheat dries in the field and the cisterns go empty. The people came to a man named Honi and asked him to pray for rain. He prayed, and nothing happened.

So Honi drew a circle on the ground and stood inside it. He spoke to God, as the Mishnah tells it, like a child speaking to a parent. He swore he would not step out of the circle until God showed mercy to the people. A few drops fell. Honi said this was not what he had asked for.

Then the rain poured so hard that people feared floods. Honi said this was not what he had asked for either. He asked for rain of goodwill and blessing, and it came gently. The story is in Mishnah Ta'anit 3:8, and the Talmud later tells more of Honi's life.

Not everyone was pleased. Simeon ben Shetach, the head of the court, sent Honi a message. If you were not Honi, he said, I would put you under a ban. But what can I do? You act before God like a child who gets whatever he asks. The Mishnah keeps both the miracle and the complaint.
story.think: Why do you think the Mishnah keeps Simeon ben Shetach's complaint instead of telling only the miracle?

lessons.title: A Tractate Called Fast
lessons.mainIdea: Tractate Ta'anit, meaning Fast, sets out the public fasts a community held when the rain did not come.
reading: *Ta'anit* means fast. It is a tractate in the order of Moed, the order about set times and holidays. Most of it deals with a problem every farmer in ancient Israel knew. The rainy season comes in the fall and winter. If the rain was late, the whole year's food was at risk.

Mishnah Ta'anit chapter 1 lays out steps. If the rain had not come by a certain date in the fall, some individuals began to fast. If there was still no rain, the court declared public fasts for the community. Each round was stricter than the one before. The Mishnah describes the steps with care, like a plan for an emergency.

The rabbis treated drought as more than bad weather. Rabbinic tradition reads the Torah's promise of rain in its season, in Deuteronomy 11, as tied to the people's conduct. A public *fast* was a way to stop, look at how the community was living, and pray together. Modern readers differ on how to read that link, and many focus on the fast as a call for shared action.

words.d: Fast; a tractate in the order Moed about public fasts, mostly for rain
going without food and drink for a set time, often with prayer
Set Times; the order of the Mishnah about Shabbat and holidays
a long time without enough rain

lessons.title: Sackcloth or Deeds?
lessons.mainIdea: On a public fast day the Mishnah has an elder remind the people that God saw Nineveh's deeds, not only its fasting.
reading: Mishnah Ta'anit 2:1 describes a public fast day. The ark with the Torah scroll was brought out to the town square. Ashes were put on it and on the heads of the leaders. Then the eldest among them spoke words meant to move the crowd and turn their minds to how they lived.

The elder said: our brothers, it does not say of the people of Nineveh that God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says God saw their deeds, that they turned from their evil way. He was quoting Jonah 3:10. In the book of Jonah, the city of Nineveh changes how it lives, and the threatened punishment does not come.

The point is sharp. A fast without changed behavior is empty, the Mishnah suggests. The words teach *teshuvah*, turning or repentance, as action, not just feeling. Readers link this teaching to the prophets, such as Isaiah 58, which asks for a fast that feeds the hungry and frees the oppressed.

words.d: turning or repentance; changing one's ways
the city in the book of Jonah whose people change their ways

lessons.title: Nakdimon and the Borrowed Water
lessons.mainIdea: Ta'anit 19b–20a tells how Nakdimon ben Gurion borrowed water for pilgrims and how rain came just in time.
reading: The Gemara on Ta'anit tells a story set in Jerusalem while the Temple still stood. Pilgrims had come for a festival, and there was no water to drink. Nakdimon ben Gurion, a rich man of the city, went to a Roman official who owned water. He borrowed twelve wells of water for the pilgrims.

Nakdimon promised to give back twelve wells of water by a set day, or pay a huge sum of silver. The day came, and the wells were still empty. The official mocked him. Nakdimon went to the Temple, wrapped himself in his prayer shawl and prayed. The sky filled with clouds, and rain filled the wells.

The official claimed the sun had already set, so the deadline was past. Nakdimon prayed again, and the clouds parted so the sun shone. The Talmud says that is how he got his name, from a word for breaking through. This is *aggadah*, story in the Talmud. Readers take it as a lesson about generosity for strangers and about prayer, while scholars study it as legend.

words.d: the story and teaching parts of the Talmud, as opposed to law
people who travel to a holy place for a festival
the discussion and commentary on the Mishnah that makes up most of the Talmud

lessons.title: Standing in the Circle
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Ta'anit 3:8 tells how Honi drew a circle and would not leave it until rain came in the right measure.
reading: Honi is called *ha-Me'aggel*, the circle-drawer. Mishnah Ta'anit 3:8 tells his most famous story. The people asked him to pray for rain, and nothing came. He drew a circle, stood in it, and swore by God's great name not to move until God had mercy on the people.

The rain came in three kinds. First a few drops; Honi said he had not asked for that. Then a pounding storm; he had not asked for that either. At last he asked for rain of goodwill, blessing and grace, and the right rain fell. The story shows prayer as a kind of bold conversation.

The historian Josephus, writing in Greek in the first century CE, mentions a man called Onias who was known for praying for rain. Many scholars think Onias and Honi are the same man, and they date him to the first century BCE. The Mishnah and Josephus tell different stories about him, so historians read both with care.

words.d: Honi the circle-drawer, a figure of the 1st century BCE known for prayers for rain
a Jewish historian of the 1st century CE who wrote in Greek
a solemn promise, often made by naming God

lessons.title: The Complaint of Simeon ben Shetach
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah keeps Simeon ben Shetach's criticism of Honi next to the miracle, so the argument stays in the text.
reading: After the rain, Simeon ben Shetach sent Honi a message. Simeon was head of the court and one of the pairs in Avot. He said that if Honi were anyone else, he would have put him under a *ban*, a formal punishment that kept a person apart from the community.

Then Simeon quoted Proverbs 23:25: let your father and mother be glad. He compared Honi to a son who nags his father until the father gives him what he wants. The words are part praise and part worry. Honi had been close to God, Simeon admitted, but he had also made demands and sworn an oath he might not keep.

Readers split on how to take this. Some say the Mishnah admires Honi's closeness to God. Others say it warns against treating prayer like a bargain. Many teachers point to the structure: the Mishnah records the miracle and the objection together. That habit of keeping both voices is one of the Talmud's marks.

words.d: a formal punishment by a rabbinic court that kept a person apart from the community for a time
head of the court in the 1st century BCE, one of the pairs named in Avot
a challenge raised against a statement or act

lessons.title: The Carob Tree and Seventy Years
lessons.mainIdea: In Ta'anit 23a Honi sleeps seventy years, and the story ends with the saying "either friendship or death."
reading: The Gemara in Ta'anit 23a tells a longer tale. Honi saw a man planting a carob tree. He asked how long until it gave fruit. Seventy years, the man said. Honi asked if he expected to live that long. The man said: I found carob trees in the world. As my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children.

Then Honi sat down to eat and fell asleep. A rock formed around him, and he slept for seventy years. When he woke, he saw the grandson of the planter gathering carobs. He went to the study hall and heard the students say their teachings were as clear as in Honi's day. He said he was Honi, but no one believed him or gave him honor.

Honi was so hurt that he prayed to die, and he died. The Gemara says that Rava drew a lesson: either *chavruta* or death, meaning either companionship or death. A chavruta is a study partner. The story is read as about planting for the future and as about how people need to be known by others.

words.d: a study partner; also companionship; Talmud is often studied in pairs
a tree whose pods are eaten; the story says it takes seventy years to bear fruit
a Babylonian amora of the 4th century CE

lessons.title: The Day and the Sick
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Yoma 8 rules that a person in danger is fed on Yom Kippur and that rubble is cleared on Shabbat to save a life.
reading: *Yoma*, meaning The Day, is the tractate about Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Most of it describes the high priest's service in the Temple. Its last chapter turns to the fast. Mishnah Yoma 8:6 says that a sick person is fed on Yom Kippur if experts say it is needed.

Mishnah Yoma 8:7 goes further. If a building falls on someone, and it is not known whether the person is alive, or even who the person is, the rubble is cleared on Shabbat. If the person is alive, they dig on. Doubt is not a reason to wait; doubt is a reason to act.

The rabbis call this *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life. Rabbinic law holds that it comes before almost every other command, even Shabbat and Yom Kippur. There are a few exceptions the Talmud names elsewhere, such as not killing another person to save oneself. The rule shows the course's thread of mercy written into law.

words.d: The Day; the tractate about Yom Kippur, in the order Moed
saving a life; in rabbinic law it comes before almost every other command
the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and prayer
Jewish law as the rabbis develop it; literally the way to walk

lessons.title: Where Do We Learn It?
lessons.mainIdea: In Yoma 85a–b the rabbis agree that saving a life overrides Shabbat and argue over which verse proves it.
reading: Yoma 85a tells of three sages walking together: Rabbi Ishmael, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva. A question was put to them. Where do we learn that saving a life pushes aside Shabbat? They all agreed on the rule. What they argued about was the proof.

Rabbi Ishmael pointed to the Torah's law of a thief breaking in, in Exodus 22. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah reasoned from *brit milah*, circumcision, which is done on Shabbat. If one part of the body overrides Shabbat, he said, surely the whole body does. That is a *kal va-chomer*, an argument from the lighter case to the heavier one.

Rabbi Akiva argued from Exodus 21 and the altar. Then the Gemara on 85b brings more proofs. One rabbi reads Exodus 31:16: break one Shabbat for a person so he can keep many Shabbatot. Each proof is tested and challenged. This is a *sugya* in motion: question, proof, objection and answer, all on behalf of a life.

words.d: a unit of Talmudic discussion on one question
an argument from a lighter case to a heavier one, in English a fortiori
circumcision, done on the eighth day even when it falls on Shabbat
a verse or teaching brought to support a ruling

lessons.title: Live by Them
lessons.mainIdea: Shmuel reads Leviticus 18:5 as "live by them, and not die by them," and Rava says this proof cannot be refuted.
reading: Near the end of the sugya, Rav Yehudah reports a teaching of Shmuel, a Babylonian *amora* of the third century. Shmuel cited Leviticus 18:5: you shall keep My laws, which a person shall do and live by them. The rabbis read "live by them" as "and not die by them."

Shmuel said that if he had been there, he would have had a better proof. Rava later said that every other proof could be challenged, but Shmuel's could not. The earlier proofs only work when a life is certainly at risk. "Live by them" covers even a case of doubt, like the rubble in Mishnah Yoma 8:7.

Centuries later, Maimonides wrote in his law code that the Torah's laws are not meant as vengeance on the world but as mercy, kindness and peace. He also said that the leaders of the community, not strangers or children, should do the work of saving a life on Shabbat. Jewish readers across movements cite this teaching in hospitals and emergency services today.

words.d: a teacher of the Gemara, active c. 200–500 CE
a Babylonian amora of the 3rd century CE, a colleague of Rav
Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), who wrote the law code Mishneh Torah

lessons.title: What Yom Kippur Cannot Do
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teaches that Yom Kippur atones for wrongs against God, but wrongs against people need reconciliation first.
reading: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 draws a firm line. For wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur brings *atonement*. For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone until the wrongdoer makes peace with the one who was hurt. The day alone is not enough.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah drew this from Leviticus 16:30: from all your sins before the LORD you shall be clean. He read "before the LORD" as limiting the verse. Only sins before God alone are cleared by the day. A verse's small phrase becomes a large ethical rule, which is a common Talmudic move.

This Mishnah shapes how many Jews prepare for Yom Kippur. In the days before it, many people ask family, friends and coworkers for *forgiveness*. Rabbinic tradition puts the burden on the one who did wrong. It is not enough to feel sorry in private; the hurt person has to be approached and set right.

words.d: being cleared of a wrong; making amends
letting go of blame toward someone who did wrong
to make peace again after a wrong

lessons.title: Law, Story and Mercy Together
lessons.mainIdea: Ta'anit and Yoma mix law and story, and both keep asking what a rule protects: the hungry town, the person under rubble, the one who was wronged.
reading: The two tractates in this chapter do not keep *halakhah* and aggadah apart. Ta'anit gives rules for public fasts, then tells of Honi and Nakdimon. Yoma describes the Temple service, then rules on saving a life and on asking forgiveness. Law and story sit on the same page and shed light on each other.

Look at who each passage protects. The fasts protect a town facing hunger. Honi's story asks for rain of blessing, not a flood. Mishnah Yoma 8:7 protects a stranger under rubble, even if no one knows who he is. Yoma 8:9 protects the person who was hurt, by making the one who hurt them come and make it right.

Readers across Judaism draw different lessons. Orthodox readers often stress the precise rules for when a life overrides Shabbat. Conservative and Reform readers often stress the ethics behind them. Academic scholars study how the stories and laws grew. All of them read the same pages, and that shared reading is part of the Talmud's life.

words.d: Jewish law as the rabbis develop it; literally the way to walk
the story and teaching parts of the Talmud
kindness shown to someone in need or in one's power
